title: When the Autopsy Burns Revisited
premise: Estate lawyer Wren Okafor, who has spent a decade hiding his own past behind procedural precision, is named executor of a will for a woman he never represented—a will dated three days after her death. A confession letter arrives postmarked the day after her funeral, naming Wren as the recipient of a ledger that records the town's quiet crimes, including the drowning the police ruled an accident twenty years ago. As Wren decodes the ledger's cipher hidden in probate filings, he realizes the dead woman was protecting him specifically: she witnessed the crime that made him flee his hometown and change his name. The tide that took one body finally gives up another, forcing Wren to choose between the anonymity he built and the justice the law can no longer deliver.
about_author: Odile Halloran spent fifteen years as a coastal coroner's assistant before turning to fiction, a career that taught her how often the dead outlast their secrets. She writes from a rented cottage above a tidal estuary, where she keeps a weathered tide table pinned above her desk.

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't Filed
chapters.summary: Wren Okafor, POV. Wren receives a probate packet for Marguerite Voss, a client he never had, containing a will executed after her death certificate. His meticulous routine cracks as he notices his own name in the executor clause. Emotional beat: unease—the first hairline fracture in his carefully invisible life.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. At the funeral of a woman he never met, Wren learns from the grieving nephew that Marguerite spoke his name on her last night. That evening a letter arrives, postmarked the day after the funeral, confessing to 'what the tide took' and promising him a ledger. Beat: dread sharpening into compulsion.

chapters.title: Ledger Hidden in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Back at his office, Wren discovers the 'ledger' is encoded across decades of probate filings—account numbers, dates, and estate values forming a cipher. The first decoded entry names a drowned boy: Daniel Reyes, 2004, ruled accidental. Beat: cold recognition; Wren knew that name once.

chapters.title: The Man He Used to Be
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Wren's POV. Twenty years earlier: a frightened teenager leaving Saltmere Bay under a new name after witnessing something on the pier. Present-day Wren confronts how thoroughly he buried this self. Beat: grief and shame surfacing like a body in shallow water.

chapters.title: The Nephew Who Counts Too Well
chapters.summary: Nephew Theo Voss, POV. Theo, an accountant, suspects the estate's numbers don't reconcile and begins pulling the same filings Wren decoded. He resents the stranger executor but is drawn to the puzzle. Beat: rivalry seeded; two readers converging on one hidden text.

chapters.title: Entries in Red Ink
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Decoded entries reveal a pattern: payments to officials, a silenced witness, and Marguerite's own signature as both recorder and payer. Someone has been checking the files before Wren—pages subtly reordered. Beat: paranoia; the archive itself feels watched.

chapters.title: Saltmere Bay at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren returns to Saltmere Bay for the first time in two decades, renting a room under his real surname for the first time since fleeing. The pier, the estuary, the old Reyes house—memory and geography collide. Beat: vertigo of belonging to a place that remembers you.

chapters.title: What the Harbor Master Kept
chapters.summary: Harbor master Ilsa Brandt, POV. Ilsa, Marguerite's old friend, recognizes Wren instantly and says nothing—yet. Her chapters reveal she helped Marguerite build the ledger and mailed the letter on instructions left in a safe-deposit box. Beat: loyalty divided between the dead and the living.

chapters.title: A Confession With Two Authors
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Forensic details in the confession letter don't match Marguerite's handwriting samples in the estate file. Part of it was written by someone else—someone still alive, still local. Beat: the mystery pivots from what happened to who is steering him now.

chapters.title: Theo Finds Entry Forty-One
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Theo independently cracks part of the cipher and finds entry forty-one: a payment to a police sergeant the week after Daniel Reyes drowned. He photographs the page and hesitates over whether to send it to anyone—or use it. Beat: temptation; justice and leverage blur.

chapters.title: The Sergeant's Widow
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren interviews the widow of Sergeant Cole Hargrave, who died last spring. She is polite, terrified, and lets slip that her husband kept 'a box for Marguerite.' That night someone searches Wren's rental room. Beat: the hunt reverses—he is being hunted.

chapters.title: Rising Water
chapters.summary: Ilsa, POV. Ilsa warns Wren away from the estuary boathouse where the final ledger pages are hidden, then contradicts herself by drawing him a tide chart. Her ambivalence breaks open: she believes Marguerite's death was not natural. Beat: alliance formed in guilt.

chapters.title: Entry Fifty-Two: My Own Name
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Decoding deeper, Wren finds entry fifty-two—a payment made to keep a teenage witness silent. The witness was him. Marguerite paid to save his life, which means she knew his identity all along and chose him deliberately as executor. Beat: devastating reframe of his whole exile.

chapters.title: The Boathouse at Slack Tide
chapters.summary: Wren and Ilsa, alternating POV. They retrieve a waterproof case from the boathouse floor containing Marguerite's original journal and a second confession—written by Cole Hargrave before his death, admitting the cover-up but not the killing. Beat: triumph curdling; they have half the truth.

chapters.title: Someone Else Read It First
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Theo confronts Wren with photographs of the journal pages—taken days ago. The pages are now blank where entries fifty-three onward should be. Someone with access beat them there. Beat: betrayal and urgency; the clock is the tide itself.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Last Week
chapters.summary: Ilsa, POV. Ilsa reconstructs Marguerite's final days: a visitor from out of town, a burned letter in the hearth, and a phone call about 'the boy from the pier.' The visitor signed the guestbook with a name Wren recognizes from the ledger. Beat: the killer acquires a face.

chapters.title: The Man Who Paid for Silence
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. The surviving conspirator is revealed: councilman Aldous Penhale, whose fortune was built on the harbor development that required Daniel Reyes's silence—and whose son, not Hargrave, held the boy under. Penhale offers Wren money and a clean exit. Beat: moral nadir; the price of staying invisible, itemized.

chapters.title: What Wren Owes the Dead
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Alone with Marguerite's journal, Wren reads her account of watching him flee and deciding, twenty years too late, to spend her last months making it right. He drafts two documents: a resignation as executor, and a full disclosure affidavit. Beat: resolve; identity chosen, not fled to.

chapters.title: Storm Surge
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. Penhale moves to destroy the remaining evidence stored in the estuary archive as a storm floods the coast; Theo, Ilsa, and Wren race the water separately, each holding a piece. Beat: climax rising—nature, greed, and truth all converging on one night.

chapters.title: What the Tide Gives Up
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. In the flooded archive, Wren corners Penhale retrieving the final pages. The confrontation turns violent; Ilsa and Theo arrive, and Penhale's own recorded confession—left running on Theo's phone—becomes the evidence. The receding tide exposes Daniel Reyes's missing shoe, buried in the pilings. Beat: climax; the sea testifies.

chapters.title: Probate in Open Court
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Months later: Penhale indicted, the fraudulent will ratified by a judge sympathetic to its intent, and Wren testifying under his real name, surrendering the anonymity he built. The ledger becomes public record. Beat: catharsis through exposure; justice outside the law feeding back into it.

chapters.title: Executor's Final Accounting
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren settles the estate, funds a scholarship in Daniel Reyes's name, and stays in Saltmere Bay—renting, then buying, the cottage above the estuary. A letter arrives postmarked tomorrow. He opens it smiling. Beat: belonging earned; the story closes on a door left deliberately ajar.
